text: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (17 October 1817 – 27 March 1898), also spelled Sayyid Ahmad Khan, was an Indian Muslim reformer, philosopher, and educationist in the 19th-century British Raj. Initially advocating Hindu–Muslim unity, he later became the pioneer of Islamic reformism and Muslim nationalism in India and is widely credited as the father of the two-nation theory, which formed the basis of the Pakistan Movement. He founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh, the first Muslim university in Southern Asia, and was awarded an honorary LLD from the University of Edinburgh in 1889. Born in Delhi to Syed Muhammad Muttaqi and Aziz-un-Nisa, he was the youngest of three siblings and raised in a wealthy area of the city under the influence of his maternal grandfather Khwaja Fariduddin, who served as Wazir in the court of Emperor Akbar Shah II, and his paternal grandfather Syed Hadi Jawwad bin Imaduddin, who held a high-ranking mansab position in the court of Emperor Alamgir II. His father, Syed Muhammad Muttaqi, was a personal adviser to Emperor Akbar Shah II. Sir Syed received a traditional Muslim noble education, studying the Qur'an, Persian, and Arabic, and was taught mathematics, astronomy, and algebra; he also studied medicine under Hakim Ghulam Haider Khan and was skilled in swimming and shooting. His early writings, influenced by Sufism, Shah Waliullah, and the Mujahidin movement, focused on reforming Muslim practices and promoting the purity of Islamic belief. Over time, his views evolved due to exposure to Western thought, particularly the Utilitarians like John Stuart Mill and the essays of Joseph Addison and Richard Steele. He began writing religious treatises in 1842, including Jila al-Qulub bi Zikr al-Mahbub, Tuhfa-i Hasan, Kalimat al-Haqq, and Rah i Sunna dar radd i Bid'a, and later authored Tabyin Al-Kalam, a Muslim commentary on the Tawrat and Injeel, considered the first systematic effort at interfaith dialogue in India. In response to Christian missionary activities and British historical portrayals of Islam, he wrote Tabin al-al-kalam Fi tafsir altawrat Wa ‘I-injil’ala millat al Islam (1862–1865), a commentary on the Torah and Gospel from a Muslim perspective. He also engaged with Darwinian ideas, adopting a theistic evolutionist view supported by Islamic scholars like Al-Jahiz and Ibn Khaldun. In 1877, he began working on a Quranic commentary, Tafsir ul-Quran, which was published in seven volumes, with the first volume appearing in 1880 and the last published in 1904, six years after his death. He served in various judicial roles, including as a Serestadar, Munsif, and Sadr Amin, and was promoted to Sub-Judge of Small Causes in 1864. During the Indian Rebellion of 1857, he remained loyal to the British Raj and saved many European lives in Bijnor. He was appointed Sadarus Sudoor in 1858 and later served in Ghazipur and Aligarh. In 1869, he accompanied his son to England to gain firsthand knowledge of Western civilization. He retired from government service in 1876 and settled in Aligarh, where he served in the Imperial Legislative Council from 1878 to 1880 and again until 1883, and in the Legislative Council of the Lieutenant Governor of the North-Western Provinces from 1887 to 1893. Despite criticism from figures such as Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Husayn Batalwi, and Qasim Nanautawi, Sir Syed is recognized as a pioneer of Muslim modernism and educational reform. His advocacy of rationalism, a neo-Mu'tazilite understanding of Islamic scripture, questioning the authenticity of many Hadith, rejecting ijma (consensus), broadening ijtihad (independent reasoning), and interpreting Biblical scripture from a Muslim perspective, continues to influence global Islamic reformation. He became a source of inspiration for the Pakistan Movement and its leaders, including Allama Iqbal and Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Many universities and public buildings in Pakistan bear his name, and Aligarh Muslim University celebrated his 200th birth centenary on 17 October 2017. He died in 1898 and was buried at Aligarh. He once stated, "Do not show the face of Islam to others; instead show your face as the follower of true Islam representing character, knowledge, tolerance and piety."

In 1864, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan published a work titled Mahomet, which deeply distressed him due to Muir's portrayal of Islam and the character of Muhammad, as he feared it might create doubts among young Muslims. To gain a firsthand understanding of Western civilisation, he accompanied his son to England. He was also a reader of Darwin and, while not fully agreeing with all of his ideas, aligned himself with a theistic evolutionist view similar to that of Asa Gray, one of the first Islamic scholars to adopt this perspective. His arguments were based on his own scientific research and quotes from earlier Islamic scholars such as Al-Jahiz, Ibn Khaldun, and Shah Waliullah. In 1877, he began working on a tafsir, or commentary on the Quran, which was published in seven volumes: the first volume appeared in 1880, and the last was released six years after his death in 1904. This work analyzed and interpreted 16 paragraphs and 13 surahs of the Quran, with the first volume including a detailed article titled Tahrir fi Usool al-Tafsir, outlining 15 principles for his commentary. Sir Syed’s preferred field of study was history; in 1840, he compiled chronological tables on the Timurid rulers of Delhi, later published as Jam-i-Jum (Jamshed's Cup), and in Silsilat-ul-Mulk, he compiled biographical data on all Delhi rulers. During his time in Bijnor, he wrote a history of the city, which was destroyed during the 1857 rebellion. He also produced critical editions of Ziauddin Barani's Tarikh-e-Firoz Shahi (1862) and Tuzk-e-Jahangiri (1864). His most significant historical works, which established his scholarly reputation, were the two editions of Asar-us-Sanadid and the edition of the Ain-e-Akbari. In 1847, he published Asar-us-Sanadid, divided into four sections: one on buildings outside Delhi, one on those around the Delhi Fort, one on monuments in Shahjahanabad, and one on the historical settlements and prominent inhabitants of Delhi, including Sufis, physicians, scholars, poets, calligraphers, and musicians. The work included around 130 illustrations drawn by Faiz Ali Khan and Mirza Shahrukh Beg, the first lithographically produced book illustrations in India. A second edition, released in 1854, was abbreviated and more factual, bringing him wider fame and earning him recognition as a cultured scholar. In 1861, it was translated into French by Gracin de Tassy in Paris and presented to the Royal Asiatic Society, making him an honorary fellow. In 1855, he completed his illustrated edition of Abul Fazl's Ain-e-Akbari, with the first and third volumes published in 1855 and the second volume, sent in 1857, destroyed during the 1857 rebellion. He approached Mirza Asadullah Khan Ghalib to write a taqriz for the work, but Ghalib responded with a Persian poem criticizing the Ain-e-Akbari and the Mughal culture it represented, calling it of little value and reprimanding Syed Ahmad Khan for wasting his time on "dead things," while praising the "sahibs of England." After this, Sir Syed never again wrote in praise of the Ain-e-Akbari and abandoned active interest in history and archaeology, though he edited two other historical texts later, neither of which matched the scale or ambition of the Ain-e-Akbari. During the 1857 uprising, Sir Syed served as a chief assessment officer in Bijnor and recorded the mutiny in Tarikh i Sarkashi-ye Bijnor, published in 1858. He was deeply concerned about the consequences for Muslims and wrote several articles and pamphlets, including Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (The Causes of the Indian Revolt), Loyal Muhammadans of India, and a review of Dr. Hunter's Indian Musalmans: Are They Bound in Conscience to Rebel Against the Queen? to defend Muslims and Islam and foster good relations with British authorities. He supported the East India Company during the uprising, a stance criticized by some nationalists like Jamaluddin Afghani. In 1859, he published Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind in Urdu, rejecting the idea that Muslim elites planned the revolt, instead blaming the East India Company’s aggressive expansion and British ignorance of Indian culture. He advised the British to appoint Muslims to administrative roles to prevent what he called ‘haramzadgi’ (a vulgar deed) such as the mutiny. Maulana Altaf Hussain Hali wrote that upon reaching Muradabad, Sir Syed began writing Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind to clear Muslims of mutiny accusations, despite the danger, and refused to accept British theories. After completing the work, he sent the Urdu version to the Mufassilat Gazette Press in Agra, receiving 500 copies back. A friend, Rae Shankar Das, warned him not to send it to the British Parliament or government, urging him to burn the copies. Sir Syed replied that he was bringing the matter to the British for the good of his people, the country, and the government, and was willing to suffer harm if it benefited all. Das wept and remained silent after seeing Sir Syed’s resolve. After performing a supplementary prayer, Sir Syed sent nearly all 500 copies to England, one to the government, and kept the rest. When the government translated and presented the pamphlet to the council, Lord Canning and Sir Bartle Frere accepted it as sincere and friendly, though Foreign Secretary Cecil Beadon attacked it as "an extremely seditious pamphlet," demanding a proper inquiry and harsh treatment for the author. Since no other council member agreed with him, his criticism caused no harm. Later, at Lord Canning’s durbar in Farrukhabad, Beadon expressed displeasure and said he would have communicated his views directly to the government if he truly cared for the government’s interests. Sir Syed responded that only 500 copies were printed, most sent to England, one given to the government, and the rest still in his possession, with proof of distribution. He noted that the rulers’ views had been distorted by the anxieties of the time and promised to personally pay 1,000 rupees for every copy found circulating in India. Beadon initially doubted this, repeatedly asking Sir Syed, but after reassurance, he never mentioned it again and later became one of Sir Syed’s strongest supporters. Many official translations of Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind were made, including one by the India Office that sparked debate. The government of India and several members of parliament also translated it, though no public version was offered. A translation started by Auckland Colvin was completed by Sir Syed’s friend, Colonel G.F.I. Graham, and published in 1873. In 1860, Sir Syed published a series of bilingual pamphlets, Risala Khair Khwahan-e Musalmanan-e-Hind (An Account of the Loyal Mohammedans of India) from Meerut, in three issues—first and second in 1860, third in 1861. The first issue highlighted the bravery of Muslims loyal to the British, while the second included an article on jihad, clearly distinguishing it from rebellion. In August 1871, William Wilson Hunter published Indian Musalmans: Are They Bound in Conscience to Rebel Against the Queen?, linking the Indian Wahabi movement to rebellion and calling them self-styled jihadis, which led to the prosecution of Muslims, especially in the North-West Provinces. This prompted Sir Syed to write a rebuttal, published in The Pioneer from 24 November 1871 to 23 February 1872, later collected and published in England by Hafiz Ahmad Hasan. He based his arguments on Muhammad’s conduct during holy wars. Throughout the 1850s, Sir Syed developed a strong passion for education, realizing the benefits of Western-style education offered at newly established colleges in India. Despite being a devout Muslim, he criticized traditional dogma and religious orthodoxy, which had made many Indian Muslims suspicious of British influences. As a scion of Mughal nobility, he was aware of the decline of Muslim political power and feared that the animosity between the British and Muslims before and after the 1857 rebellion would marginalize Muslim communities. He intensified efforts to promote cooperation with British authorities and loyalty to the Empire among Indian Muslims. In 1859, he founded a modern madrassa in Muradabad, one of the first religious schools to offer scientific education. He also helped organize relief for famine-struck people in the North-West Province in 1860. While posted in Ghazipur in 1863, he established a madrasa that later became Victoria High School and formed the Scientific Society in Ghazipur to promote educational reforms. He wrote an insightful tract on education titled Iltimas Ba Khidmat-e-Sakinan-e-Hind Dar Bab-e- Taraqqi Taleem in Ahl-e-Hind (Address to the natives of Hindoostan on education). Upon his transfer to Aligarh in 1864, he worked wholeheartedly as an educator. The Scientific Society was moved to Aligarh and renamed the Scientific Society of Aligarh, modeled after the Royal Society and the Royal Asiatic Society. It held annual conferences, disbursed funds for educational causes, and published a journal on scientific subjects in English and Urdu. Sir Syed believed that the socio-economic future of Muslims was threatened by their orthodox aversion to modern science and technology. He published many writings promoting liberal, rational interpretations of Islamic scriptures, striving to find rational explanations for jinn, angels, and the miracles of the prophets. One example was his argument in the tafsir that riba referred to interest charges when lending money to the poor, but not to the rich or borrowers in trade or industry, since such finance supported trade, national welfare, and prosperity. While many jurists declared all interest as riba, Sir Syed argued this was based on their own authority and deduction, not the Quran. On 1 April 1869, he traveled to England with his sons Syed Mahmood and Syed Hamed, where he was awarded the Order of the Star of India on 6 August. During his visit, he visited English colleges and was inspired by the post-Renaissance culture of learning. Upon returning to India, he determined to build a school modeled on Cambridge and Oxford to impart modern education. On 26 December 1870, he established the Khwastgaran-i-Taraqqi-i-Talim-i-Musalman (Committee for the Better Diffusion and Advancement of Learning among Muhammadans), which by 1872 was converted into a Fund Committee for establishing a school. In an article written in 1872 and reprinted in the Aligarh Institute Gazette on 5 April 1911, Sir Syed described his vision of a university similar to Oxford or Cambridge, with mosques attached to each college, a dispensary with a doctor and compounder, and a Unani Hakim. Boys in residence were required to attend congregational prayers at all five times, with students of other religions exempted. Muslim students wore a black alpaca, half-sleeved chugha, and a red Fez cap. Bad and abusive language, including the word "liar," was strictly prohibited. Food was served on European-style tables or Arab-style chaukis. Smoking cigarettes or huqqa and chewing betel were strictly prohibited. Corporal punishment or any punishment likely to injure a student’s self-respect was forbidden. Shia and Sunni boys were prohibited from discussing their religious differences in the college or boarding house. He began publishing the journal Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq on 24 December 1870 to spread awareness of modern subjects and promote social reforms in Muslim society.

Students of other religions will be exempted from attending prayers (namaz) at all five times, while Muslim students will wear a uniform consisting of a black alpaca, half-sleeved chugha, and a red Fez cap. Bad and abusive words, including the term "liar," will be strictly prohibited. Students will have food either on European-style tables or on chaukis in the Arab manner. Smoking cigarettes or huqqa and chewing betels are strictly prohibited. No corporal punishment or any form of punishment likely to injure a student's self-respect will be allowed. It will be strictly enforced that Shia and Sunni boys shall not discuss their religious differences in the college or boarding house. Sir Syed began publishing the journal Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq on 24 December 1870 to spread awareness of modern subjects and promote Muslim societal reforms. He advocated for a reinterpretation of Muslim ideology to reconcile tradition with Western education, arguing that the Qur'an emphasizes reason and natural law, making scientific inquiry essential for a good Muslim. By 1873, a committee under Sir Syed proposed building a college in Aligarh, with Maulvi Samiullah Khan appointed as secretary of the sub-committee. The committee toured the country to raise funds, and the school was established on 24 May 1875 in Aligarh as the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental Collegiate School. In 1877, it was converted into the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College. Sir Syed retired from his legal career the following year to focus entirely on the college and religious reform. His work received support from the British, though it faced intense criticism from orthodox Muslim leaders hostile to modern influences. The college attracted a large student body, mainly from the Muslim gentry and middle classes, and was open to all communities, including a significant number of Hindu students; the first graduate was a Hindu. The curriculum included scientific and Western subjects, as well as Oriental and religious education. The first chancellor was Sultan Shah Jahan Begum, a prominent Muslim noblewoman, and Sir Syed invited Theodore Beck, an Englishman, as the first principal. The college was initially affiliated with Calcutta University and transferred to Allahabad University in 1885. Near the turn of the 20th century, it began publishing its own magazine and established a law school. In 1920, it was transformed into Aligarh Muslim University. To promote his movement, Sir Syed founded the All India Muhammadan Educational Congress in Aligarh, with its first session held in 1886 under Maulvi Samiullah Khan’s presidency. The main objective was to promote Muslim educational development through conferences and to transform the Anglo-Oriental College into a university. The organization was renamed the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference to avoid confusion with the Indian National Congress. Sir Syed's efforts were opposed by orthodox Indian Muslims; Imdad Ali, the deputy collector of Kanpur, condemned the college's foundation. Periodicals such as Noor-ul-Afaq, Noor-ul-Anwar, and Taed-ul-Islam were launched by opponents to counter Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq. Many orthodox Islamic schools condemned him as a kafir (unbeliever), and J.M.S. Baljon noted that his ideas triggered "a real hurricane of protests and outbursts of wrath" among clerics across Muslim India, who issued fatawa declaring him a kafir. He was also accused of converting to Christianity, and Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, founder of the Ahmadiyya movement, criticized his writings in a work titled Barakat al Dua. Jamal al-Din al-Afghani attacked him as a "Naturist" in a periodical. His own friends, such as Nawab Muhsin-ul-Mulk, expressed reservations about his religious views, particularly those in his Qur'anic commentary. His rejection of miracles, denial of angels, and downplaying of prophethood drew disdain from reformist groups like Ahl-e Hadith and Deobandis, with leaders like Muḥammad Ḥusayn Baṭālvī declaring Takfir (excommunication) of Sir Syed. Maulana Qasim Nanautawi, founder of Darul Uloom Deoband, expressed admiration for Sir Syed’s courage and concern for Muslims but voiced deep complaints about his "disturbed" beliefs in a letter, later published as "Tasfiyat ul Aqaaid" in 1887. Shan Muhammad notes Sir Syed was primarily an educationist and reformer, not an academic thinker, and his political views were shaped by events such as the 1857 Rebellion, William Ewart Gladstone’s premiership (starting in 1868), and the viceroyalty of Ripon. Sir Syed was deeply religious, with political views centered on Islam. In 1878, he was nominated to the Viceroy's Legislative Council and testified before the education commission to promote more colleges and schools. Early in his political career, he advocated Hindu-Muslim unity and India’s composite culture, wanting to empower all Indians. In the same year, he founded the Muhammadan Association to promote political cooperation among Indian Muslims. In 1886, he organized the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference in Aligarh to promote modern education and Muslim political unity. He became the most prominent Muslim politician in 19th-century India, influencing Muslim attitudes on national issues. Sir Syed discouraged Muslim political involvement, prioritizing higher English education over political pursuits. He declined to support the National Muhammadan Association founded by Syed Ameer Ali in 1887 and refused to participate in the Muhammedan National Conference at Lahore, which he viewed as a political agitation. When the Indian National Congress was established in 1885, he did not express an opinion, but later became an active critic and opponent. Maulvi Sharaf-ul-Haqq criticized his views on Congress demands in a risala titled Kalam Mufid-al-Anam, and Lala Lajpat Rai wrote open letters expressing grief and surprise at his shift. Sir Syed supported constitutional methods, such as participation in administration, to express grievances to the British government. He backed efforts by Surendranath Banerjee and Dadabhai Naoroji to secure Indian representation in government and civil services. In 1883, he founded the Muhammadan Civil Service Fund Association to support Muslim graduates entering the Indian Civil Service (ICS). In the same year, he established the Muhammadan Association to present Muslim grievances to the Imperial Legislative Council. He was nominated to the Civil Service Commission in 1887 by Lord Dufferin. In 1888, he co-founded the United Patriotic Association with Raja Shiv Prasad of Benaras to promote political cooperation with the British and Muslim participation in British governance. Sir Syed advocated Hindu-Muslim unity in colonial India, stating: "India is a beautiful bride and Hindus and Muslims are her two eyes. If one of them is lost, this beautiful bride will become ugly." Raised in Delhi, he was exposed to both Hindu and Muslim festivals, collected Hindu scriptures, and maintained close friendships with Swami Vivekanand and Debendranath Tagore. He opposed cow slaughter, even stopping a fellow Muslim from sacrificing one for Eid al-Adha to promote peace. In a speech in Gurdaspur on 27 January 1884, he said: "O Hindus and Muslims! Do you belong to a country other than India? Don't you live on the soil and are you not buried under it or cremated on its ghats? If you live and die on this land, then bear in mind that ‘Hindu’ and ‘Muslim’ is but a religious word: all the Hindus, Muslims and Christians who live in this country are one nation." When founding the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, he opened admissions to all faiths, with its first principal, Henry Siddons, being a Christian and one of its patrons, Mahendra Singh of Patiala, being a Sikh. Shafey Kidwai notes Sir Syed promoted the empowerment of all Indians. In his book Causes of the Indian Revolt (originally published in Urdu in 1858), he referred to Hindus and Muslims as 'two antagonistic races' when criticizing British efforts to unite them. The onset of the Hindi–Urdu controversy in 1867 saw Sir Syed emerge as a champion of the Urdu language. He opposed the adoption of Hindi as a second official language in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh), viewing Urdu as the lingua franca created from Muslim and Hindu contributions during the Mughal period. He promoted Urdu through his writings and had the Scientific Society translate Western works only into Urdu. Schools established by Sir Syed provided education in Urdu. The demand for Hindi, driven largely by Hindus, was seen by Sir Syed as a threat to centuries-old Muslim cultural dominance. Before the British education commission, he controversially stated that "Urdu was the language of gentry and Hindi that of the vulgar," provoking strong opposition from Hindu leaders who united to demand Hindi recognition. The success of the Hindi movement led Sir Syed to further advocate Urdu as a symbol of Muslim heritage and the language of all Indian Muslims. His educational and political work increasingly focused on Muslim interests. He sought British support for extensive official use and patronage of Urdu. Colleagues like Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Maulvi Abdul Haq formed organizations such as the Urdu Defence Association and the Anjuman Taraqqi-i-Urdu to preserve Urdu. These efforts led to Urdu being adopted as the official language of Hyderabad State and as the medium of instruction in Osmania University. To Muslims in northern and western India, Urdu became an integral part of political and cultural identity. The division over Hindi or Urdu intensified communal conflict between Muslims and Hindus. Sir Syed is considered the first to theorize Muslim separate nationhood in the subcontinent. In a 1888 speech at Meerut, he described Muslims and Hindus as two nations. He is regarded as the father of the two-nation theory and the pioneer of Muslim nationalism, which led to the partition of India. The Urdu-Hindi controversy is seen as the turning point in Sir Syed's views on Muslim nationhood, expressed in later speeches. While fearing loss of Muslim political power due to backwardness, he was also opposed to democratic self-government, which would give control to the Hindu-majority population. He stated: "At this time our nation is in a bad state in regards education and wealth, but God has given us the light of religion and the Quran is present for our guidance, which has ordained them and us to be friends. Now God has made them rulers over us. Therefore we should cultivate friendship with them, and should adopt that method by which their rule may remain permanent and firm in India, and may not pass into the hands of the Bengalis... If we join the political movement of the Bengalis our nation will reap a loss, for we do not want to become subjects of the Hindus instead of the subjects of the 'people of the Book'." Later, he said: "Suppose that the English community and the army were to leave India, taking with them all their cannons and their splendid weapons and all else, who then would be the rulers of India? Is it possible that under these circumstances two nations — the Mohammedans and the Hindus — could sit on the same throne and remain equal in power? Most certainly not. It is necessary that one of them should conquer the other. To hope that both could remain equal is to desire the impossible and the inconceivable. But until one nation has conquered the other and made it obedient, peace cannot reign in the land." In 1836, he married Parsa Begum, alias Mubarak Begum. They had two sons, Syed Hamid and Syed Mahmood, and a daughter, Ameena, who died young. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan lived the last two decades of his life in Aligarh, regarded as the mentor of 19th and 20th century Muslim entrepreneurs. Battling illness and old age, he died on 27 March 1898 and was buried adjacent to the Sir Syed Masjid in the grounds of Aligarh Muslim University. He is widely commemorated across South Asia as a great Muslim social reformer and visionary. His educational model and progressive thinking inspired Muslim elites who supported the All India Muslim League. He founded the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886 to promote Western education, especially science and literature, among Muslims. The conference generated funds for the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College and motivated Muslim elites to expand educational uplift, known as the Aligarh Movement. This awareness helped stimulate political consciousness among Muslim elites, leading to the formation of the AIML, which eventually led Muslims toward the creation of Pakistan. He influenced political leaders, thinkers, and writers such as Muhammad Iqbal, Abul Kalam Azad, Sayyid Mumtaz Ali, Altaf Hussain Hali, Shibli Nomani, Nawab Mohsin-ul-Mulk, Chiragh Ali, and Nazir Ahmad Dehlvi. The university he founded remains one of India’s most prominent institutions and served as the arsenal of Muslim India. Prominent alumni include Maulana Mohammad Ali Jouhar, Abdur Rab Nishtar, Maulana Shaukat Ali, and Maulvi Abdul Haq. The first two Prime Ministers of Pakistan, Liaquat Ali Khan and Khawaja Nazimuddin, and Indian President Dr. Zakir Husain, are among the most famous graduates. His birth anniversary is celebrated as Sir Syed Day annually by the university and its alumni. Several educational institutions in India and Pakistan, such as Sir Syed University of Engineering and Technology, Sir Syed CASE Institute of Technology, and Sir Syed College, Taliparamba, are named after him. On 2 June 1869, Syed Ahmad Khan was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Star of India (CSI) for his service as Principal.

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, a prominent figure in Indian history, founded the Aligarh Muslim University, which remains one of India's most prominent institutions and served as the arsenal of Muslim India. Prominent alumni include Muslim political leaders Maulana Mohammad Ali Jouhar, Abdur Rab Nishtar, Maulana Shaukat Ali, and Maulvi Abdul Haq. The first two Prime Ministers of Pakistan, Liaquat Ali Khan and Khawaja Nazimuddin, as well as Indian President Dr. Zakir Husain, are among its most famous graduates. His birth anniversary is celebrated annually as Sir Syed Day by the university and its alumni. Several educational institutions in India and Pakistan, such as Sir Syed University of Engineering and Technology, Sir Syed CASE Institute of Technology, and Sir Syed College, Taliparamba, are named after him. On 2 June 1869, Syed Ahmad Khan was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Star of India (CSI) for his service as Principal Sadr Amin. He was appointed a fellow of the Calcutta and Allahabad Universities by the Viceroy in 1876 and 1887 respectively. Later, he was bestowed the suffix 'Khan Bahadur' and was knighted by the British government in the 1888 New Year Honours as a Knight Commander of the Order of the Star of India (KCSI) for his loyalty to the British crown, particularly through his membership in the Imperial Legislative Council. In the following year, he received an LL.D. honoris causa from Edinburgh University. India Post issued commemorative postage stamps in his honour in 1973 and 1998. A road named Sir Sayed Road exists in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Pakistan Postal Services issued a commemorative postage stamp in 1990 as part of its 'Pioneers of Freedom' series. In 1997, an English Heritage blue plaque was placed at 21 Mecklenburgh Square in Bloomsbury, where he lived from 1869 to 1870. On 2017, the State Bank of Pakistan issued a commemorative Rs. 50 coin on his 200th birth anniversary. On 14 August 2022, marking the diamond jubilee of Pakistan's independence, the State Bank of Pakistan released a commemorative Rs. 75 note featuring Syed Ahmed Khan alongside other founding fathers symbolizing their struggle for independence. The Urdu-language biographical film "Sir Syed Ahmad Khan: The Messiah" was released in 2024 and streamed on Apple TV.
